screens.title: Control Theory for Aerial Vehicles
screens.narratorSegment: Control theory is the toolbox we use to make a quadrotor do what we ask. In this chapter you'll learn the parts of a control loop — reference, error, controller, sensor, and plant — and how simple controllers like PD and PID stabilize a vehicle. We show practical MATLAB controller functions for altitude and attitude control, explain why a feedforward term like mass times gravity matters for hover, and examine how the integral term removes steady-state error yet can cause integrator windup when actuators saturate. You will also see trajectory generation techniques, from cubic polynomials to the minimum-snap idea that keeps acceleration continuous and motor commands realistic. Examples ground each idea: a PD altitude controller with different gain sets, an attitude controller across three axes, and a cubic trajectory generator that preserves position, velocity, and acceleration continuity. By the end you'll be able to design basic PD and PID controllers for a quadrotor and produce smooth waypoint trajectories that the vehicle can actually follow. Consider: what makes a controller both fast and stable, and how do we avoid overshoot while keeping response quick?

Control Theory for Aerial Vehicles
Design PD/PID controllers, analyze stability, and create smooth quadrotor trajectories suitable for real motors.
In this lesson

You will see how an error signal drives control actions, how proportional, derivative, and integral terms shape response, and how polynomial trajectories ensure continuous acceleration for safe flight.

Why it matters
Good control keeps a drone safe, efficient, and responsive under disturbances like wind.
What you'll practice
Tuning PD and PID gains in simulation and generating cubic trajectories through waypoints.
Explore Key Topics
Control Loop
Reference, error, controller, plant and sensor form the loop that drives convergence to the setpoint.
PD & PID
Proportional, derivative, and integral terms shape response speed, damping, and steady-state accuracy.
Trajectories
Cubic and minimum-snap polynomials ensure smooth position, velocity and acceleration profiles for flight.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Visual concept
Reference
Desired altitude or orientation.
Sensor
IMU or barometer reading the actual state.
Controller
PD or PID computing thrust and torques.
Plant
The quadrotor responds to inputs and physics like gravity and drag.
Getting started
Begin with the control loop and a PD altitude controller in simulation. Then add integral action and explore trajectory polynomials for waypoint navigation.

These skills matter because controllers translate desired flight behavior into safe actuator commands, and trajectory generation ensures commands are feasible for real motors. screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Outcomes
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus on measurable practice: simulate an altitude PD controller with ode45 and compare responses under several gain sets, then add an integral term to see steady-state correction under a constant disturbance. You will write two concise MATLAB functions: one that returns thrust for altitude with a gravity feedforward term and a separate one that computes torque commands for roll, pitch and yaw using vectorized PD control. Understanding anti-windup methods is part of the practical outcome: when the motor saturates, the integral term must not keep growing or the system will overshoot when it recovers. screens.title: Control loop components and the error signal
screens.narratorSegment: A control loop is a simple, repeating structure that turns a desired state into actuator commands that make the plant follow that state. The four canonical components are a reference or setpoint, the plant (the quadrotor), sensors that measure the current state, and the controller which computes inputs from the error. The error is simply r(t) minus y(t): the difference between what you want and what you measure. This difference is the signal the controller uses to decide how hard to act. Consider hovering: if r is z_des = 2 meters and the sensor reports z = 1.8 meters, the error is 0.2 meters. A proportional action produces a thrust command proportional to that 0.2 meter difference. A common misconception is to treat sensor readings as perfect; in practice sensors add noise and delay, and controllers must be robust to those imperfections. Another misconception is to assume the controller alone ensures safety; the plant dynamics and actuator limits must be considered too. Practically, you test the loop in simulation by applying a setpoint change and observing how the error decays. For design, always ask whether the controller reduces error reliably under small disturbances and whether the sensors and actuators can implement the commanded inputs. What steady-state behavior will you expect if disturbances persist and the controller has no integral action?

keyIdea.title: Error drives the controller
keyIdea.text: The error signal r(t)-y(t) is the single measured quantity that the controller uses to compute corrective inputs; everything in the loop exists to reduce that error.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Control loop components
Definition
What each component does
Reference (setpoint)
The desired state, for example z_des = 2 m or roll = 0 degrees.
Plant
The quadrotor and its physics; it responds to thrust and torque inputs.
Sensor
IMU, barometer and other sensors measure the plant state and can introduce noise and latency.
Controller
Computes inputs from the error e(t) = r(t) - y(t) to drive the plant toward the reference.
Key Takeaway

The error signal is the central quantity; design choices for controller, sensors, and actuators determine whether the error is reduced robustly under realistic conditions.

Concrete example
Hover setpoint z_des=2 m; measured z=1.8 m gives e=0.2 m. A proportional term produces thrust proportional to that 0.2 m error. If a persistent downward wind exists, the error will remain unless the controller has integral action to accumulate and correct steady offsets.
Misconception
Sensors are not perfect. Treat measurements as noisy and delayed; controllers should avoid overreacting to instantaneous sensor noise.
Try this
In simulation, add sensor noise and a small time delay and observe how the closed-loop response changes. Note how derivative action reacts to noisy signals.
Check

What happens if the controller ignores actuator limits? The controller could command unattainable inputs and integral accumulation could worsen overshoot once saturation clears.

screens.title: PD controller: proportional and derivative action
screens.narratorSegment: A PD controller combines a proportional action that pushes toward the setpoint with a derivative action that resists motion. Mathematically, u(t) = Kp * e(t) + Kd * de(t)/dt. The proportional term responds to the magnitude of the error: larger error produces larger corrective input. The derivative term responds to the speed of change of the error and acts like a damper, reducing overshoot and oscillation. A useful physical analogy is a mass attached to a spring and a damper: the spring provides a restoring force proportional to displacement (the proportional term) and the damper resists velocity (the derivative term). In design, Kp controls how aggressively the system moves to the reference, while Kd controls the damping and reduces oscillatory behavior. One common misconception is to think increasing Kd always improves behavior; excessive derivative can amplify sensor noise and make the controller jitter. A concrete example is altitude control: with Kp small and Kd zero you may see sustained oscillations; increase Kd to damp those oscillations but avoid too large a Kd if your sensor is noisy. When tuning, watch settling time, overshoot, and steady-state behavior. How would you trade off a faster rise time against larger overshoot in a quadrotor?

keyIdea.title: PD intuition
keyIdea.text: Kp determines responsiveness to error magnitude while Kd shapes damping by resisting rapid error changes; together they produce a damped response.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › PD Controller
Process: PD action
How proportional and derivative terms combine
Formula
u(t) = Kp * e(t) + Kd * de(t)/dt
Spring-damper analogy
Proportional is like a spring force; derivative is like a damper resisting velocity to reduce overshoot.
Design notes
  • Increase Kp for faster response but watch for oscillation.
  • Add Kd to damp oscillations, but be cautious with noisy sensors.
  • Check step responses to compare rise time and overshoot.
Concrete example: altitude
If you apply a PD law to altitude, a small Kp with no Kd often yields oscillation. Adding Kd damps vertical motion and reduces overshoot. Observe with four gain sets in simulation: the change in Kp and Kd changes stability and settling time.
Common Mistake
Applying large derivative gains without filtering sensor noise can make inputs jitter and destabilize the system.
Key Takeaway

Use Kp for speed and Kd for damping. Tune them together and always consider sensor noise when adding derivative action.

screens.title: Altitude PD controller (MATLAB example)
screens.narratorSegment: This lesson walks through a concise MATLAB altitude controller used for a quadrotor hover. The code computes the altitude error between desired and current position, applies proportional correction, and subtracts a derivative term scaled by vertical velocity. Importantly it includes a feedforward component m*g that provides thrust to counteract gravity so the controller only corrects deviations. The function returns thrust u which the plant uses in dynamics. Reading code in small functions helps you reason about each term separately. For an example, the function sets e_z = z_des - z, then u = m*g + Kp_z*e_z - Kd_z*z_dot. If z_dot is positive upward velocity, the derivative reduces thrust when climbing and increases thrust when descending, damping vertical motion. A common misconception is to omit the feedforward term and expect the proportional term alone to hold hover; without m*g the controller must generate a continuous offset which can lead to larger gains and worse performance. Use this pattern as a template: separate feedforward physics from corrective feedback so tuning focuses on error correction rather than supporting basic equilibrium. Altitude PD controller (MATLAB example) means include physics-based feedforward such as m*g for hover, then apply pd corrections to handle deviations and damping.. In practical terms, feedforward gravity with proportional and derivative corrections. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Feedforward + PD
keyIdea.text: Include physics-based feedforward such as m*g for hover, then apply PD corrections to handle deviations and damping.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Altitude PD Controller
MATLAB function
This snippet returns total thrust including feedforward gravity and PD corrections.
<!-- Escaped MATLAB code -->
function u = altitude_controller(z, z_dot, z_des, Kp_z, Kd_z, m, g)
    e_z = z_des - z;
    u = m*g + Kp_z * e_z - Kd_z * z_dot;
end
Notes: the m*g term supplies hover thrust; Kp_z corrects altitude error; -Kd_z*z_dot damps vertical motion.
Concrete walkthrough
If z_des=5 m and current z=4.8 m, e_z=0.2 m, Kp_z*e_z increases thrust to climb. If the vehicle is already moving upward, the -Kd_z*z_dot term subtracts thrust to prevent overshoot. The net thrust combines physics and corrections.
Misconception
Dropping the feedforward term forces the controller to hold hover via offset in Kp, making tuning and disturbance rejection harder.
Try this in sim

Run an ode45 simulation using this controller and compare responses with and without m*g in the control law. Observe steady offsets and required gain sizes.

screens.title: Attitude PD controller for roll, pitch and yaw
screens.narratorSegment: Attitude control treats roll, pitch and yaw as separate channels that can often be controlled with parallel PD loops. The MATLAB pattern is concise and vectorized: compute the angle error vector between desired and measured angles, then compute torque as tau = Kp.* e - Kd.* angles_dot. This yields an independent PD action per axis, which simplifies implementation and tuning in many quadrotor controllers. The proportional term pushes each axis toward its setpoint while derivative action damps rotational velocity. A concrete example: if the desired roll is zero and the vehicle is rolled by five degrees with a nonzero roll rate, the PD torque on that axis combines a restorative torque proportional to five degrees and a damping torque opposing the current roll rate. A common misconception is to assume strong coupling is always negligible; aerodynamic effects and cross-coupling can influence axes, but for many small quadrotor designs independent PD channels are effective. When tuning, start with small Kp, increase until you see oscillation, then add Kd to damp. Vectorized code helps maintain concise functions and consistent behavior across all three axes.

keyIdea.title: Parallel axis control
keyIdea.text: Treat roll, pitch, and yaw as three PD channels with vector operations to compute torque commands for each axis.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Attitude PD Controller
MATLAB pattern
<!-- Escaped MATLAB code -->
function tau = attitude_controller(angles, angles_dot, angles_des, Kp, Kd)
    e = angles_des - angles;
    tau = Kp .* e - Kd .* angles_dot;
end
This uses element-wise operations to compute torques for roll, pitch and yaw simultaneously.
Concrete scenario
Suppose angles_des = [0;0;0] and measured roll = 5 degrees with roll rate nonzero. The error produces a restorative torque on roll, and derivative action opposes the roll rate. Repeat similar logic for pitch and yaw.
Misconception
Treating axes as fully decoupled ignores aerodynamic and inertial coupling. Verify independence in simulation before assuming no cross-coupling on hardware.
Key Takeaway

Vectorized PD controllers simplify implementation and provide separate tuning knobs per axis, but validate coupling effects for your vehicle.

screens.title: PID controller and the integral term
screens.narratorSegment: A PID controller extends PD with an integral term that accumulates error over time. The controller law becomes u(t) = Kp * e(t) + Ki * integral of e(t) dt + Kd * de/dt. The integral term corrects steady-state errors that arise from persistent disturbances or model mismatch. For example, if wind provides a constant downward force and a PD controller cannot fully counter it, the integral term will slowly increase control effort until the altitude error is eliminated. That is powerful, but it brings the risk of integrator windup: if actuators saturate while the integral still accumulates, a large stored integral can cause excessive overshoot when saturation clears. Anti-windup techniques prevent accumulation when the actuator is at its limit or clamp the integral term to a safe range. Another misconception is to expect the integral term to speed up transient response; in fact, integral tends to act slowly and improves steady-state accuracy rather than transient speed. When adding Ki, retune Kp and Kd since the integrator changes closed-loop dynamics. A practical rule: add a small Ki only after you have acceptable damping and rise time with PD terms, then slowly increase Ki until steady-state error disappears without introducing significant overshoot.

keyIdea.title: Integral fixes offsets
keyIdea.text: Ki accumulates persistent error to eliminate steady-state offsets, but requires anti-windup strategies when actuators saturate.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › PID Controller
Definition
Proportional, integral and derivative terms combined
Formula
u(t) = Kp*e(t) + Ki*∫e(t)dt + Kd*de(t)/dt
Role of integral
Accumulating error until steady offsets are corrected; essential under constant disturbances.
Integrator Windup
When actuators saturate, continued accumulation causes large stored integral and later overshoot. Use clamping or conditional integration to prevent it.
Concrete example
Introduce a downward disturbance of 0.5 N while hovering. A PD controller will leave a steady offset. Adding Ki gradually increases thrust until the offset disappears. Watch how Ki must be moderate to avoid slow oscillatory behavior.
Key Takeaway

Use integral action to remove steady-state error, but design anti-windup and retune PD gains after adding Ki.

screens.title: Integrator windup and anti-windup strategies
screens.narratorSegment: Integrator windup occurs when the controller's integral term continues to accumulate error while the actuator cannot respond because it is saturated at its limit. Imagine the motors are at maximum thrust during a large disturbance: the integral keeps growing because the error remains, and when the actuator is no longer saturated the accumulated integral can drive a large corrective surge that causes overshoot. Two straightforward anti-windup strategies help: clamping the integral term within bounds, and conditional integration where you stop integrating when the actuator is saturated in the direction of the integral. Both techniques limit the stored integral and avoid large rebounds. In practice choose limits based on actuator capability and the expected maximum steady correction. A misconception is to treat anti-windup as optional; on real platforms actuator saturation is common, so anti-windup is a necessary safety measure. When testing in simulation, intentionally saturate actuators to validate anti-windup behavior and measure overshoot with and without anti-windup. Which anti-windup method suits your control architecture will depend on simplicity versus responsiveness and how gracefully you want the system to recover after long saturation events.

keyIdea.title: Prevent overshoot after saturation
keyIdea.text: Limit or pause the integral when actuators saturate to prevent large accumulated corrections and subsequent overshoot.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Integrator Windup
What happens
When actuator limits are reached, the integral keeps accumulating error and leads to large stored corrections that cause overshoot when the actuator recovers.
Clamping
Limit the integral term to specified min and max values so it cannot grow unbounded during saturation.
Conditional integration
Pause integrating while the actuator is saturated and the integral would increase the saturation further.
Concrete validation
In simulation, saturate thrust at a realistic motor maximum and compare responses with no anti-windup, clamped integral, and conditional integration. Measure overshoot and recovery time to select the best approach for your quadrotor.
Misconception
Anti-windup is not only for extreme events; even moderate saturation during maneuvers can accumulate integral and produce poor behavior.

screens.title: PID tuning methods
screens.narratorSegment: Tuning PID gains balances speed, damping, and robustness. The chapter outlines three approaches: Ziegler–Nichols, manual tuning, and optimization in simulation. Ziegler–Nichols is an experimental recipe that helps find initial gains by pushing the proportional gain until sustained oscillation, then computing Kp, Ki and Kd from that critical point. Manual tuning is iterative: start with small Kp, increase until you see oscillation, then add Kd to damp and finally add Ki to remove steady-state error. Optimization uses simulations and a chosen performance metric like minimal settling time or minimal overshoot to search for gains automatically. Each method has trade-offs: Ziegler–Nichols is fast for initial guesses but can produce aggressive gains; manual tuning is intuitive but time-consuming; optimization can produce tailored gains but requires a reliable model and objective. A common mistake is to tune solely on idealized models without testing disturbances, sensor noise, or actuator limits. Always validate tuned gains under realistic disturbances and with actuator saturation. Practically, combine methods: use Ziegler–Nichols or a coarse optimization to get a starting point, then refine manually while watching real-world constraints. narration.text: Tuning PID gains balances speed, damping, and robustness. The chapter outlines three approaches: Ziegler–Nichols, manual tuning, and optimization in simulation. Ziegler–Nichols is an experimental recipe that helps find initial gains by pushing the proportional gain until sustained oscillation, then computing Kp, Ki and Kd from that critical point. Manual tuning is iterative: start with small Kp, increase until you see oscillation, then add Kd to damp and finally add Ki to remove steady-state error. Optimization uses simulations and a chosen performance metric like minimal settling time or minimal overshoot to search for gains automatically. Each method has trade-offs: Ziegler–Nichols is fast for initial guesses but can produce aggressive gains; manual tuning is intuitive but time-consuming; optimization can produce tailored gains but requires a reliable model and objective. A common mistake is to tune solely on idealized models without testing disturbances, sensor noise, or actuator limits. Always validate tuned gains under realistic disturbances and with actuator saturation. Practically, combine methods: use Ziegler–Nichols or a coarse optimization to get a starting point, then refine manually while watching real-world constraints. Comparison of methods
Ziegler–Nichols
Experimental method to find initial gains using the critical oscillation point. Good for starting values but can be aggressive.
Manual tuning
Iterative, intuitive approach: increase Kp, add Kd for damping, then Ki for steady-state. Requires patience and validation.
Optimization
Use simulation and an objective like minimum settling time or minimal overshoot to find gains, assuming an accurate model.
Practical guidance
Start conservative, validate under disturbances and actuator limits, and prefer gradual refinement. Use simulation cases like the four altitude gain sets from the chapter to compare behavior.
Misconception
A single tuning method is sufficient for all scenarios. In practice combine methods and validate for realistic disturbances and limits.

screens.title: Trajectory generation with cubic polynomials
screens.narratorSegment: Trajectory generation builds a time-parameterized path the quadrotor can follow. Cubic polynomials are a simple, practical choice when you want continuous position, velocity and acceleration at endpoints. The cubic trajectory formula uses boundary conditions: initial and final positions and velocities, and a total duration. The code in the chapter computes polynomial coefficients a0.. a3 based on p0, p1, v0, v1 and T, then evaluates position, velocity and acceleration at time t. Continuous acceleration is important because motor commands depend on acceleration; discontinuous acceleration implies infinite jerk and is not physically realizable. A concrete example: moving from p0 to p1 over T seconds with zero initial and final velocity yields a smooth takeoff and stop with no abrupt acceleration spikes. A common misconception is that higher-order polynomials always improve tracking; while higher order can shape snap and jerk better, they require more constraints and care. Cubic polynomials are simple to implement and verify. When implementing, sample pos, vel, acc across time and inspect plots for smoothness before commanding the vehicle. What constraints would you add if you needed bounded acceleration or limited maximum thrust?

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Cubic Trajectories
MATLAB cubic generator
<!-- Escaped MATLAB code -->
function [pos, vel, acc] = cubic_trajectory(p0, p1, v0, v1, T, t)
    % p0, p1: initial and final positions
    % v0, v1: initial and final velocities
    % T: total duration
    % t: current time (0 <= t <= T)
    
    a0 = p0;
    a1 = v0;
    a2 = (3*(p1 - p0) - T*(2*v0 + v1)) / T^2;
    a3 = (2*(p0 - p1) + T*(v0 + v1)) / T^3;
    
    pos = a0 + a1*t + a2*t^2 + a3*t^3;
    vel = a1 + 2*a2*t + 3*a3*t^2;
    acc = 2*a2 + 6*a3*t;
end
This produces continuous pos, vel and acc across the interval [0,T]. Verify by plotting pos, vel and acc against time.
Why continuous acceleration matters
Motors and propellers cannot instantaneously change thrust. Continuous acceleration avoids commanding infinite jerk and keeps actuator demands feasible.
Misconception
Higher-order polynomials always solve problems. They add complexity and require more constraints; start with cubic for typical waypoint transitions.
Key Takeaway

Use cubic polynomials when you need smooth position, velocity and acceleration profiles with minimal constraints and simple implementation.

screens.title: Minimum-snap trajectories and practical considerations
screens.narratorSegment: Minimum-snap trajectories extend polynomial trajectory design by minimizing the integral of the snap, which is the fourth derivative of position. Minimizing snap produces smoother higher derivatives like jerk and acceleration profiles, which is especially beneficial for quadrotors because motor commands depend on acceleration and rapid changes produce demanding motor behavior. Typically minimum-snap uses higher-order polynomials with constraints at waypoints for position, velocity and acceleration, and an objective that minimizes integrated snap subject to those constraints. The result is a trajectory that is smooth up through high derivatives and reduces actuator stress and control effort. However, minimum-snap is more complex to implement than simple cubic polynomials and requires solving an optimization problem, often offline or in a computationally efficient form. A common misconception is that minimum-snap always yields better performance; while it reduces high-frequency demands, it also requires accurate modeling and careful constraint choice. In practice use minimum-snap for aggressive waypoint sequences where jerk and snap would otherwise cause unacceptable motor commands, and use cubic polynomials for simpler transitions. Minimum-snap minimizes the integrated fourth derivative of position, producing trajectories with smooth acceleration and reduced high-frequency actuation.

Aggressive waypoint transitions or when actuator stress from abrupt commands must be minimized.

screens.title: Simulate altitude control with ode45
screens.narratorSegment: The hands-on activity in the chapter walks you through a MATLAB simulation using ode45 to compare altitude responses for several PD gain combinations, and then extends the controller to PID under a constant disturbance. Begin by implementing the altitude_controller function that returns thrust as m*g + Kp*e - Kd*z_dot. Implement a simple quadrotor vertical dynamics model where the acceleration equals (u - m*g - disturbance)/m. Run ode45 from initial z=0 with z_des=5 m and simulate four gain sets: (1) Kp=1, Kd=0 showing unstable oscillation; (2) Kp=5, Kd=2 showing stable but slow response; (3) Kp=10, Kd=5 showing faster response with some overshoot; (4) Kp=20, Kd=8 showing fast response with minimal overshoot. Plot z(t) for all cases on one figure to compare. After comparing PD results, add Ki=2 and a constant downward disturbance of 0.5 N. Observe how PID eliminates steady-state error that PD cannot. A common mistake is to compare plots without normalizing axes or without including actuator limits. Make sure to model thrust saturation to see integrator windup and then implement clamping to prevent it. What effect does adding Ki have on peak overshoot in your plots?

keyIdea.text: Run parallel simulations for multiple gain sets, then add an integral term and disturbance to observe steady-state correction and the need for anti-windup.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Hands-on: ode45
Activity steps
  1. Implement altitude_controller as shown previously with feedforward m*g and PD terms.
  2. Model vertical dynamics: m * z_ddot = u - m*g - disturbance (apply saturation if desired).
  3. Run ode45 for t in [0,T] from z=0 to z_des=5 m with four gain sets and plot z(t) together.

Plot four z(t) curves with distinct colors. Label overshoot and settling. Then add PID curve under disturbance to show zero steady-state error.

How did adding Ki affect overshoot and recovery? Use that observation to decide whether to reduce Ki or increase Kd in your next tuning iteration.

fullNarratorScript:
Control theory is the toolbox we use to make a quadrotor do what we ask. In this chapter you'll learn the parts of a control loop — reference, error, controller, sensor, and plant — and how simple controllers like PD and PID stabilize a vehicle. We show practical MATLAB controller functions for altitude and attitude control, explain why a feedforward term like mass times gravity matters for hover, and examine how the integral term removes steady-state error yet can cause integrator windup when actuators saturate. You will also see trajectory generation techniques, from cubic polynomials to the minimum-snap idea that keeps acceleration continuous and motor commands realistic. Examples ground each idea: a PD altitude controller with different gain sets, an attitude controller across three axes, and a cubic trajectory generator that preserves position, velocity, and acceleration continuity. By the end you'll be able to design basic PD and PID controllers for a quadrotor and produce smooth waypoint trajectories that the vehicle can actually follow. Consider: what makes a controller both fast and stable, and how do we avoid overshoot while keeping response quick?

By the end of this chapter you will design and tune PD and PID controllers for a quadrotor's attitude and altitude, reason about stability using damping and natural frequency ideas, and create smooth trajectories between waypoints. You will also learn to write simple MATLAB controller functions that include a feedforward gravity term for hover and to simulate closed-loop altitude responses using ordinary differential equation solvers. These skills matter because controllers translate desired flight behavior into safe actuator commands, and trajectory generation ensures commands are feasible for real motors. A concrete example you will practice is building an altitude PD controller, running four tuning cases that show unstable oscillation, slower settling with damping, and faster responses with some overshoot. You will also extend that controller to PID, introduce a constant disturbance, and observe how the integral term eliminates steady-state error. Finally, you will generate a cubic polynomial trajectory and inspect position, velocity, and acceleration continuity to ensure the vehicle never receives abrupt demands. Which of these objectives will you try first in simulation?

These objectives focus on measurable practice: simulate an altitude PD controller with ode45 and compare responses under several gain sets, then add an integral term to see steady-state correction under a constant disturbance. You will write two concise MATLAB functions: one that returns thrust for altitude with a gravity feedforward term and a separate one that computes torque commands for roll, pitch and yaw using vectorized PD control. You will also generate a cubic polynomial trajectory between two waypoints and examine its position, velocity and acceleration at intermediate times to confirm smoothness. Understanding anti-windup methods is part of the practical outcome: when the motor saturates, the integral term must not keep growing or the system will overshoot when it recovers. Practically, you will practice clamping the integral or pausing integration during saturation. These skills let you move from conceptual analysis to implementing stable closed-loop behaviors in simulation before testing on hardware.

A control loop is a simple, repeating structure that turns a desired state into actuator commands that make the plant follow that state. The four canonical components are a reference or setpoint, the plant (the quadrotor), sensors that measure the current state, and the controller which computes inputs from the error. The error is simply r(t) minus y(t): the difference between what you want and what you measure. This difference is the signal the controller uses to decide how hard to act. Consider hovering: if r is z_des = 2 meters and the sensor reports z = 1.8 meters, the error is 0.2 meters. A proportional action produces a thrust command proportional to that 0.2 meter difference. A common misconception is to treat sensor readings as perfect; in practice sensors add noise and delay, and controllers must be robust to those imperfections. Another misconception is to assume the controller alone ensures safety; the plant dynamics and actuator limits must be considered too. Practically, you test the loop in simulation by applying a setpoint change and observing how the error decays. For design, always ask whether the controller reduces error reliably under small disturbances and whether the sensors and actuators can implement the commanded inputs. What steady-state behavior will you expect if disturbances persist and the controller has no integral action?

A PD controller combines a proportional action that pushes toward the setpoint with a derivative action that resists motion. Mathematically, u(t) = Kp * e(t) + Kd * de(t)/dt. The proportional term responds to the magnitude of the error: larger error produces larger corrective input. The derivative term responds to the speed of change of the error and acts like a damper, reducing overshoot and oscillation. A useful physical analogy is a mass attached to a spring and a damper: the spring provides a restoring force proportional to displacement (the proportional term) and the damper resists velocity (the derivative term). In design, Kp controls how aggressively the system moves to the reference, while Kd controls the damping and reduces oscillatory behavior. One common misconception is to think increasing Kd always improves behavior; excessive derivative can amplify sensor noise and make the controller jitter. A concrete example is altitude control: with Kp small and Kd zero you may see sustained oscillations; increase Kd to damp those oscillations but avoid too large a Kd if your sensor is noisy. When tuning, watch settling time, overshoot, and steady-state behavior. How would you trade off a faster rise time against larger overshoot in a quadrotor?

This lesson walks through a concise MATLAB altitude controller used for a quadrotor hover. The code computes the altitude error between desired and current position, applies proportional correction, and subtracts a derivative term scaled by vertical velocity. Importantly it includes a feedforward component m*g that provides thrust to counteract gravity so the controller only corrects deviations. The function returns thrust u which the plant uses in dynamics. Reading code in small functions helps you reason about each term separately. For an example, the function sets e_z = z_des - z, then u = m*g + Kp_z*e_z - Kd_z*z_dot. If z_dot is positive upward velocity, the derivative reduces thrust when climbing and increases thrust when descending, damping vertical motion. A common misconception is to omit the feedforward term and expect the proportional term alone to hold hover; without m*g the controller must generate a continuous offset which can lead to larger gains and worse performance. Use this pattern as a template: separate feedforward physics from corrective feedback so tuning focuses on error correction rather than supporting basic equilibrium. Altitude PD controller (MATLAB example) means include physics-based feedforward such as m*g for hover, then apply pd corrections to handle deviations and damping.. In practical terms, feedforward gravity with proportional and derivative corrections. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Attitude control treats roll, pitch and yaw as separate channels that can often be controlled with parallel PD loops. The MATLAB pattern is concise and vectorized: compute the angle error vector between desired and measured angles, then compute torque as tau = Kp.* e - Kd.* angles_dot. This yields an independent PD action per axis, which simplifies implementation and tuning in many quadrotor controllers. The proportional term pushes each axis toward its setpoint while derivative action damps rotational velocity. A concrete example: if the desired roll is zero and the vehicle is rolled by five degrees with a nonzero roll rate, the PD torque on that axis combines a restorative torque proportional to five degrees and a damping torque opposing the current roll rate. A common misconception is to assume strong coupling is always negligible; aerodynamic effects and cross-coupling can influence axes, but for many small quadrotor designs independent PD channels are effective. When tuning, start with small Kp, increase until you see oscillation, then add Kd to damp. Vectorized code helps maintain concise functions and consistent behavior across all three axes.

A PID controller extends PD with an integral term that accumulates error over time. The controller law becomes u(t) = Kp * e(t) + Ki * integral of e(t) dt + Kd * de/dt. The integral term corrects steady-state errors that arise from persistent disturbances or model mismatch. For example, if wind provides a constant downward force and a PD controller cannot fully counter it, the integral term will slowly increase control effort until the altitude error is eliminated. That is powerful, but it brings the risk of integrator windup: if actuators saturate while the integral still accumulates, a large stored integral can cause excessive overshoot when saturation clears. Anti-windup techniques prevent accumulation when the actuator is at its limit or clamp the integral term to a safe range. Another misconception is to expect the integral term to speed up transient response; in fact, integral tends to act slowly and improves steady-state accuracy rather than transient speed. When adding Ki, retune Kp and Kd since the integrator changes closed-loop dynamics. A practical rule: add a small Ki only after you have acceptable damping and rise time with PD terms, then slowly increase Ki until steady-state error disappears without introducing significant overshoot.

Integrator windup occurs when the controller's integral term continues to accumulate error while the actuator cannot respond because it is saturated at its limit. Imagine the motors are at maximum thrust during a large disturbance: the integral keeps growing because the error remains, and when the actuator is no longer saturated the accumulated integral can drive a large corrective surge that causes overshoot. Two straightforward anti-windup strategies help: clamping the integral term within bounds, and conditional integration where you stop integrating when the actuator is saturated in the direction of the integral. Both techniques limit the stored integral and avoid large rebounds. In practice choose limits based on actuator capability and the expected maximum steady correction. A misconception is to treat anti-windup as optional; on real platforms actuator saturation is common, so anti-windup is a necessary safety measure. When testing in simulation, intentionally saturate actuators to validate anti-windup behavior and measure overshoot with and without anti-windup. Which anti-windup method suits your control architecture will depend on simplicity versus responsiveness and how gracefully you want the system to recover after long saturation events.

Tuning PID gains balances speed, damping, and robustness. The chapter outlines three approaches: Ziegler–Nichols, manual tuning, and optimization in simulation. Ziegler–Nichols is an experimental recipe that helps find initial gains by pushing the proportional gain until sustained oscillation, then computing Kp, Ki and Kd from that critical point. Manual tuning is iterative: start with small Kp, increase until you see oscillation, then add Kd to damp and finally add Ki to remove steady-state error. Optimization uses simulations and a chosen performance metric like minimal settling time or minimal overshoot to search for gains automatically. Each method has trade-offs: Ziegler–Nichols is fast for initial guesses but can produce aggressive gains; manual tuning is intuitive but time-consuming; optimization can produce tailored gains but requires a reliable model and objective. A common mistake is to tune solely on idealized models without testing disturbances, sensor noise, or actuator limits. Always validate tuned gains under realistic disturbances and with actuator saturation. Practically, combine methods: use Ziegler–Nichols or a coarse optimization to get a starting point, then refine manually while watching real-world constraints. PID tuning methods means combine heuristics, manual adjustments, and simulation-based optimization, and always validate gains with disturbances and actuator limits.. In practical terms, ziegler–nichols, manual tuning, and optimization trade-offs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Trajectory generation builds a time-parameterized path the quadrotor can follow. Cubic polynomials are a simple, practical choice when you want continuous position, velocity and acceleration at endpoints. The cubic trajectory formula uses boundary conditions: initial and final positions and velocities, and a total duration. Minimum-snap trajectories extend polynomial trajectory design by minimizing the integral of the snap, which is the fourth derivative of position. Minimizing snap produces smoother higher derivatives like jerk and acceleration profiles, which is especially beneficial for quadrotors because motor commands depend on acceleration and rapid changes produce demanding motor behavior. Typically minimum-snap uses higher-order polynomials with constraints at waypoints for position, velocity and acceleration, and an objective that minimizes integrated snap subject to those constraints. The result is a trajectory that is smooth up through high derivatives and reduces actuator stress and control effort. However, minimum-snap is more complex to implement than simple cubic polynomials and requires solving an optimization problem, often offline or in a computationally efficient form. A common misconception is that minimum-snap always yields better performance; while it reduces high-frequency demands, it also requires accurate modeling and careful constraint choice. In practice use minimum-snap for aggressive waypoint sequences where jerk and snap would otherwise cause unacceptable motor commands, and use cubic polynomials for simpler transitions.
